newsitem.title: USA: U.S. payrolls growth points to above-target Q4 GDP.
newsitem.headline: U.S. payrolls growth points to above-target Q4 GDP.

text.p: Stronger-than-expected job creation and a longer workweek in December will likely signal economic growth of close to 4.0 percent in the fourth quarter, U.S. economists said on Friday.

"Total hours worked is a proxy for Gross Domestic Product," said Cary Leahey, an economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc. "And these numbers would suggest growth in the area of 3.5 to 4.0 percent, much higher than target."
December nonfarm payrolls rose 262,000, far higher than the 192,000 seen by economists in a Reuters poll.
Further, factory payrolls rose 19,000 -- a figure most forecasters expected to see come in at up 10,000. The average workweek stretched to 34.8 hours from 34.5 hours in November.

"It's hard to find any good news in these numbers," Leahey added, referring to the potential impact on the U.S. Treasury market. "The totals were much higher even allowing for milder weather creating more construction jobs and the election creating more government jobs."
Prices of U.S. Treasury securities plummeted more than a full point as the strong payrolls report roiled the market.
"Initially the market's reacting to the stronger numbers and the hours worked being up," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Leahey said that while he didn't believe the Federal Reserve would move to tighten because of the data at its next meeting, he said the figures would certainly put policymakers into the frame of mind to consider doing so in March.

The Fed's policy making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets on February 4 and 5. Many analysts believe policymakers were looking to December's jobs report to assess just how strong the economy grew in the fourth quarter.

"This was an absolutely huge report in every sense of the word. It puts us at 3.0 percent growth in the fourth quarter and, more likely, closer to 3.5 percent," said Mary Dennis, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co.

With the strength seen in the overall number, upward revisions from prior months and a large increase in factory jobs, Dennis also predicted that December industrial production figures due out next Friday would come in at a 0.7 percent increase and that capacity utilization would rise to 83.7 percent from 83.3 percent in November.
Dennis said the numbers were indicative of orders demand increasing at a time when inventories were lean, meaning production will have to be stepped up.
Last week saw a strong report on the manufacturing sector from the National Association of Purchasing Management and the 19,000 jump in factory jobs confirmed strength in that sector.
Dennis said she thought the Fed needed to see more evidence from the goods market before moving to tighten, however.
"That's where foreign buyers of American products come in," she said.
Steven Wood, economist at BA Securities Inc, said that the payroll numbers supported forecasts for fourth quarter GDP growth being 3.0 percent or higher.
"Joblessness is low and and wage inflation is accelerating. With year-on-year growth of employment at 2.1 percent, trend GDP growth should be close to 3.0 percent," Wood said.
He added that despite the surprisingly good core inflation rates at both the producer and consumer levels, the data should be troubling to the FOMC.
